19:

21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`

36: - Templates users apply repeatedly

38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general

55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```

68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.

71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.

76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.

80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```

17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
90: > Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
91: > Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).
92: 
93: ### Template
94: 
95: ```yaml
96: ---
97: name: sk-example
98: description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
99: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
100: version: 1.0.0.0
101: ---
102: ```
103: 
104: ### Key Rules
105: 
106: - **name**: Must match folder name exactly, hyphen-case only
107: - **description**: Third-person voice, single line, no `<>` brackets
108: - **allowed-tools**: Use brackets `[...]`, not comma-separated string
109: - **hard rules**: Not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects the dispatch preflight reads.
110: 
111: > **Complete Reference**: For validation rules, edge cases, array formats, and all document type frontmatter, see [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md)
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 3. SKILL TEMPLATE (WITH BUNDLED RESOURCES)
116: 
117: **Use for**: Skills with bundled resources (references, scripts, or assets)
118: 
119: **Target**: 800-2000 lines (SKILL.md <1000 lines, rest in resources)
120: 
121: **Size Constraints** (package_skill.py validation):
122: - Max 5000 words (3000 recommended)
123: - Max 3000 lines
124:

126:

129:

15: # cli-devin
16: 
17: > Delegates focused tasks to Cognition's Devin CLI: multi-model coding, subagent delegation, cloud handoff and a second opinion, all from inside your current runtime.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
22: 
23: | Aspect | What you get |
24: |---|---|
25: | **Use it for** | Cross-AI delegation: coding, review, research, subagent tasks or cloud handoff through Cognition's Devin CLI, with a second-model opinion on demand |
26: | **Invoke with** | "devin", "cognition", "cloud handoff", "subagent delegation", "second opinion" or "cross-validate", plus the router intent keywords |
27: | **Works on** | Any external runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode or raw shell) that can reach the `devin` binary |
28: | **Produces** | Code edits, structured reviews, subagent task results, cloud sessions with their own VM and web-enriched research |
29: 
30: ---
31: 
32: ## 2. OVERVIEW
33: 
34: ### Why This Skill Exists
35: 
36: A long generation, an independent review, a browser-heavy task or a security audit can drain your context window and bias your own judgment. cli-devin hands such tasks to Cognition's Devin CLI, which runs its own agent in its own context with a model of your choice. The calling AI stays the conductor. The skill exists so a second AI can work on your codebase without you switching runtimes or babysitting a session.
37: 
38: ### When To Use This Skill
39: 
40: Use cli-devin when the task benefits from a second AI perspective: an independent code review, a security audit, a generation pass, parallel research or a long-running task that should keep working after you disconnect. Do not use it for quick tasks the calling agent can finish faster, nor for interactive refinement that needs the full-screen REPL (run `devin` directly instead).
41: 
42: ### What It Does
43: 
44: The skill does five things:
45: 
46: - Routes a request through the smart router, then picks a curated model and a permission mode before dispatching with `devin -p`.
47: - Delegates to Devin's native subagents through `run_subagent`.
48: - Moves a session to the cloud with `/handoff`.
49: - Attaches MCP servers with `devin mcp add`.
50: - Continues or resumes past sessions with `devin -c` and `devin -r`.
51: 
52: Orchestrated dispatches run through the shared deep-loop runtime, which is the single execution adapter for this skill. Direct `devin -p` snippets in this README are operator reference and manual-testing examples. ROUTER.md owns the routing contract and SKILL.md the hard rules.
53: 
54: ### The Delegation Layer
55: 
56: | Capability | What the skill can operate |
57: |---|---|
58: | **Multi-model dispatch** | a curated roster of seven families (DeepSeek, Gemini, GLM-5.2, GPT-5.6 Luna Max, GPT-6 Luna Max, Grok 4.5 and 4.6, and SWE-2) chosen per dispatch with `--model` |
59: | **Subagent delegation** | read-only and full-access workers through `run_subagent`, plus custom `.devin/agents/<name>/AGENT.md` profiles |
60: | **Cloud handoff** | a cloud VM with its own shell, browser and repo access via `/handoff` |
61: | **Session management** | continue and resume workflows with `devin -c` and `devin -r <session-id>` |
62: | **MCP integration** | external MCP servers attached with `devin mcp add` and listed with `devin mcp list` |
63: 
64: Subagents take a profile, not a model. `subagent_explore` runs on the cheap default and `subagent_general` inherits the parent model. To pin a model on a write-capable subagent, define a custom profile with a `model:` field. The full roster and dispatch shapes live in `references/providers-and-models.md`.
65: 
66: ### What This Skill Does Not Own
67: 
68: - It does not replace the calling runtime. The calling AI stays the conductor and verifies every result.
69: - It does not build a second execution adapter. The shared deep-loop runtime owns process construction. ROUTER.md owns routing, and SKILL.md owns prompt construction.
70: - It never dispatches into a session already running inside Devin. A running CLI skill never dispatches itself.
71: - It does not own application-code standards. Dispatched sessions load `sk-code` for surface standards and verification.
72: 
73: ---
74: 
75: ## 3. QUICK START
76: 
77: **Step 1: Confirm the binary and the login.**
78: 
79: ```bash
80: command -v devin
81: devin auth status
82: ```
83: 
84: `command -v` prints the binary path. `devin auth status` prints the logged-in state. When the login is missing, complete it before dispatching.
85: 
86: **Step 2: Install and authenticate when missing.**
87: 
88: ```bash
89: devin setup
90: curl -fsSL https://devin.ai/install | bash
91: devin auth login
92: devin --version
93: ```
94: 
95: `devin setup` runs the interactive wizard and the one-liner installs without it. `devin auth login` opens the browser OAuth flow. The CLI does not use an API key. Use `--force-manual-token-flow` on SSH-only machines. `devin --version` prints the installed version, for example `3000.2.17`.
96: 
97: **Step 3: Run the default dispatch.**
98: 
99: ```bash
100: devin -p --model swe --permission-mode accept-edits -- "Add input validation to src/utils.ts" 2>&1
101: ```
102: 
103: The default model is `swe` (alias for `swe-2`) and the default permission mode is `accept-edits`. Success looks like the file edited in place plus a text response on stdout. `devin -p` is non-interactive and exits after one turn.
104: 
105: **Step 4: Hand a long-running task to the cloud.**
106: 
107: ```bash
108: devin -- "Fix the flaky integration tests in CI, then run the full suite to confirm"
109: ```
110: 
111: Inside the session, type `/handoff fix the flaky integration tests in CI`. The cloud session gets its own VM with a shell, browser and full repo access. It keeps working after you disconnect. Track it from the terminal or the Devin web app.
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
116: 
117: ### The Smart Router
118: 
119: The router scores the request against weighted intent signals (generation, review, research, architecture, delegation, handoff, templates, patterns) and loads the matching references. `references/cli-reference.md` and `assets/prompt-quality-card.md` load on every invocation. Two hard rules gate every dispatch: the `command -v devin` availability probe and the self-invocation guard.
120: 
121: ### The Dispatch Envelope
122: 
123: A non-interactive dispatch is one command with four load-bearing parts: the model, the permission mode, the `--` separator before the prompt and `2>&1` so errors surface. `devin -p` exits after one turn, so multi-turn work uses `devin -c` or `devin -r <session-id>`. In scripts, pass the model explicitly every time and redirect stdin from `/dev/null` inside loops so the child does not drain the loop's input.
124: 
125: ### Permission Modes as the Autonomy Lever
126: 
127: Devin has no headless reasoning-effort flag. Autonomy is set through the permission mode. `devin -p` defaults to `auto`, which is read-only, so file-modification tasks silently prompt or no-op without a higher mode.
128: 
129: | Mode | Flag value | What it approves | Use for |
130: |---|---|---|---|
131: | **Auto** | `auto` | read-only tools, prompting for writes and shell commands | review, analysis, research or security work (`devin -p` default) |
132: | **Accept Edits** | `accept-edits` | workspace edits plus read-only tools, prompting for shell | code generation and refactoring (skill default) |
133: | **Smart** | `smart` | actions a fast model judges safe | trusted workflows with judgment calls |
134: | **Dangerous** | `dangerous` | every tool without prompting | full trust, explicit user approval required |
135: 
136: The `--sandbox` flag wraps the session in OS-enforced filesystem and network boundaries. On Linux it needs `devin sandbox setup`, which installs `bwrap` and `socat`. macOS works out of the box.
137: 
138: ### The Self-Invocation Guard
139: 
140: The skill refuses to load when the calling session is itself running inside Devin. Detection reads `$DEVIN_PROJECT_DIR` and the process ancestry, then probes for active-session credentials. A circular dispatch burns tokens and never converges, so the refusal is a hard rule.
141: 
142: ### Safety Invariants
143: 
144: - Run `command -v devin` before every dispatch and refuse the route when the binary is missing.
145: - Capture stderr with `2>&1` so rate-limit messages and errors surface.
146: - Verify Devin output before applying it with syntax checks, lint, type checks or the project test suite.
147: - Include the active spec folder in the dispatch prompt so the delegated agent skips the interactive gate question.
148: - Never use `--permission-mode dangerous` without explicit user approval.
149: - Never send secrets (API keys, passwords, tokens or credentials) inside a dispatch prompt.
150: 
151: ---
152: 
153: ## 5. STRUCTURE
154: 
155: ```text
156: cli-devin/
157: +-- SKILL.md                       # Hard rules and the full rule set
158: +-- README.md                      # Overview and navigation front page
159: +-- ROUTER.md                      # Machine router: intent map, resource map and loading levels
160: +-- assets/                        # Prompt resources loaded at routing time
161: |   +-- prompt-quality-card.md     # Fast-path prompt discipline and the CLEAR check, always loaded

164: +-- changelog/                     # Versioned changelog entries, one file per release
165: +-- manual-testing-playbook/       # Devin-native manual validation scenarios
166: `-- references/                    # Deep-dive reference docs loaded by intent
167:     +-- agent-delegation.md        # Subagent profile roster, routing table and custom AGENT.md patterns
168:     +-- cli-reference.md           # CLI subcommands, flags, permission modes, auth pre-flight and troubleshooting
169:     +-- cloud-handoff.md           # /handoff mechanics, use cases and state transfer
170:     +-- devin-tools.md             # Built-in capabilities: run_subagent, /handoff, MCP and session management
171:     +-- integration-patterns.md    # Dispatch shapes and the failure-mode matrix
172:     `-- providers-and-models.md    # Single-source catalog of the curated model families, aliases and defaults
173: ```
174: 
175: | File | Role |
176: |---|---|
177: | `SKILL.md` | Hard rules and the full rule set |
178: | `ROUTER.md` | Machine router: intent map, resource map and loading levels |
179: | `README.md` | Overview and navigation front page |
180: | `hard-rules.json` | Hard-rule checks the dispatch preflight reads |
181: | `references/agent-delegation.md` | Subagent profile roster, routing table and custom AGENT.md patterns |
182: | `references/cli-reference.md` | CLI subcommands, flags, permission modes, auth pre-flight and troubleshooting, always loaded |
183: | `references/cloud-handoff.md` | `/handoff` mechanics, use cases and state transfer |
184: | `references/devin-tools.md` | Built-in capabilities: `run_subagent`, `/handoff`, MCP and session management |
185: | `references/integration-patterns.md` | Dispatch shapes and the failure-mode matrix |
186: | `references/providers-and-models.md` | Single-source catalog of the curated model families, aliases and defaults |
187: | `assets/prompt-quality-card.md` | Fast-path prompt discipline and the CLEAR check, always loaded |
188: | `assets/prompt-templates.md` | Copy-paste prompt templates for common tasks |
189: 
190: ---
191: 
192: ## 6. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
193: 
194: ### Related Skills
195: 
196: | Skill | Relationship |
197: |---|---|
198: | `cli-codex`, `cli-claude-code`, `cli-opencode`, `cli-cursor`, `cli-pi` and `cli-hermes` | sibling dispatchers in the cli-* family, one dispatch at a time unless the operator authorizes parallel |
199: | `sk-code` | owns the application-code standards a dispatched session loads for review or generation |
200: | `system-deep-loop` | owns the shared fan-out runtime that executes orchestrated cli-devin dispatches |
201: | `sk-prompt` | owns per-model prompt-craft when the target model has a profile |

205: ## 7. TROUBLESHOOTING
206: 
207: | What you see | Why | Fix |
208: |---|---|---|
209: | `command not found: devin` | CLI not installed or PATH not updated | Run `devin setup` or the install one-liner, then restart the terminal |
210: | Auth error on dispatch | Devin account OAuth not configured or expired | Run `devin auth login` (browser flow) or `devin auth login --force-manual-token-flow` on SSH machines |
211: | Task ran but no files changed | `devin -p` defaults to `auto`, which is read-only | Pass `--permission-mode accept-edits` or higher |
212: | Delegated agent stalls on a spec-folder prompt | `devin -p` cannot answer interactive questions | Pass the active spec folder with the pre-approved marker, otherwise ask the user before dispatching |
213: | Self-invocation refused | The calling session is already inside Devin | Use a different runtime or exit the Devin session first |
214: | Cloud handoff fails | Network issue or uncommitted changes block the transfer | Commit or stash the changes and verify connectivity to `app.devin.ai` |
215: | Background subagent denied tools | Background workers cannot prompt for new permissions | Pre-approve the tools in the session or resume the subagent in the foreground |
216: | Slow response | Large context or complex task | Split the task, pin `swe-2-medium` for quick edits or `swe-1-7-lightning` when latency beats cost, use `auto` for pure analysis or raise the model tier for hard reasoning |
217: | `--sandbox` not available | Platform prerequisites missing | Run `devin sandbox setup` (Linux needs `bwrap` and `socat`). macOS works out of the box |
218:

223: ## 8. FAQ
224: 
225: **Q: When should I dispatch to Devin instead of doing the work myself?**
226: 
227: A: When the task benefits from a second AI perspective or a fresh context window: independent review, generation at scale, subagent research or long-running work. If the calling agent already holds the context and can finish quickly, doing it directly is faster.
228: 
229: **Q: Which model should I pick?**
230: 
231: A: The default `swe` (alias for `swe-2`, free at 262K context) balances speed and cost. Use `gpt-5-6-luna-max` for reasoning-heavy work, `glm-5-2` for general generation, `swe-2-max` for max-effort SWE work and `swe-2-medium` for quick edits. The curated roster lives in `references/providers-and-models.md` and the full family list is available through `devin models list`.
232: 
233: **Q: Can Devin keep working after I close my laptop?**
234: 
235: A: Yes, with `/handoff`. The session moves to a cloud VM with its own shell and browser plus full repo access. It keeps running after you disconnect. Track it from the terminal or the Devin web app. Hand off only long-running, browser-dependent, CI-like or high-parallelism work.
236:

238: 
239: A: User defaults live in `~/.config/devin/config.json` and project defaults in `.devin/config.json`. Pass `--model` and `--permission-mode` explicitly in scripts so the caller's config cannot change the dispatch.

    - A persona-less dispatch runs the leaf as a generic assistant, silently dropping the agent's tool-scope, verification gates, and output contract.

### ⛔ NEVER

1. Use `--permission-mode dangerous` in a task the user has not approved it for (full shell beyond workspace = damage risk). One explicit approval covers every dispatch in that task, the default invocation included, and a new task needs a new approval. `accept-edits` (workspace edits auto-approve) does not require pre-approval.
2. Trust Devin output blindly for security-sensitive code, send sensitive data (API keys, passwords, credentials) in prompts, or hammer the API with rapid sequential calls.
3. Use Devin for tasks where context is already loaded — direct action by the calling AI is faster.
4. Assume Devin output is correct without verification — cross-reference codebase and project standards.
5. Build or maintain a packet-local Devin execution adapter; the deep-loop runtime is the execution authority.

### ⚠️ ESCALATE IF

1. Devin CLI is not installed and user has not acknowledged (provide `devin setup` or install URL).
2. Rate limits are persistently exceeded (suggest checking the Devin account's plan and usage limits).

4. Task requires `--permission-mode dangerous` and the user has not approved it for this task (describe the risks and ask once for the whole task). `accept-edits` does not require escalation.

257: 6. **Redirect devin stdin from `/dev/null` on EVERY non-interactive dispatch**, not only inside a `while read` loop, the condition this rule used to name and the reason it was skipped.
258:     Pattern: `devin -p -- "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &`. Without `</dev/null`, the backgrounded devin process inherits the loop's stdin and silently consumes the remaining lines.
259:     See `references/integration-patterns.md#background-execution` → "Silent Stdin Consumption".

514: # Redact or scrub secrets before writing the JSON payload

518:   "specFolder": "<extracted or provided by calling AI>",
519:   "user_prompts": [
520:     "<delegated task or user goal>"
521:   ],
522:   "observations": [
523:     {

525:       "title": "<short accomplishment>",
526:       "narrative": "<what changed and why it matters>",
527:       "facts": [
528:         "<verification or durable implementation detail>"
529:       ]
530:     }
531:   ],
532:   "recent_context": [
533:     {

536:     }
537:   ],

541:       "DESCRIPTION": "<what changed and why it matters>",

543:       "MODIFICATION_MAGNITUDE": "small",

546:   ],

16: # Devin CLI - Complete Command Reference
17: 
18: Open this when a dispatch misbehaves or a flag's accepted value is in doubt. The tables record what the installed binary accepts, including values its help text leaves out.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Purpose
25: 
26: Provide a comprehensive, single-source reference for all Devin CLI commands, flags, models, configuration options, permission modes, and troubleshooting guidance.
27: 
28: ### When to Use
29: 
30: - Setting up or configuring Devin CLI
31: - Looking up command-line flags, subcommands, or permission modes
32: - Troubleshooting authentication, sandbox, or session issues
33: - Configuring subagents via `.devin/agents/[name]/AGENT.md`
34: - Selecting the right permission mode for a task
35: 
36: ### Core Principle
37: 
38: Devin CLI is Cognition's terminal-based AI coding agent — a fast, minimal agent that lives both in the terminal and in the cloud. It fronts a broad multi-model surface; this skill curates seven families in scope — DeepSeek, Gemini, GLM-5.2, GPT-5.6 (Luna Max), GPT-6 (Luna Max), Grok (4.5 and 4.6), and SWE-2 (full catalog: [providers-and-models.md](./providers-and-models.md)). Devin's native Adaptive model router and its full 48-family roster remain available via `devin models list` but are out of this skill's curated scope. The skill dispatches `swe` (alias → `swe-2`) at `accept-edits` permission mode by default; users can override the model and mode. It provides direct access to multi-model coding, subagent delegation, cloud handoff, MCP integration, and session management — all governed by configurable permission modes.
39: 
40: ### Key Sources
41: 
42: | Source | URL |
43: |--------|-----|
44: | **Documentation** | [docs.devin.ai/cli](https://docs.devin.ai/cli) |
45: | **Web App** | [app.devin.ai](https://app.devin.ai) |
46: | **Runtime** | Node.js / native binary |
47: | **Version** | 3000.2.17 |
48: 
49: ---
50: 
51: ## 2. INSTALLATION
52: 
53: | Method | Command | Notes |
54: |--------|---------|-------|
55: | **Interactive setup** | `devin setup` | Wizard for auth + MCP configuration |
56: | **Direct install** | `curl -fsSL https://devin.ai/install \| bash` | Persistent install |
57: | **Update** | `devin update` | Check for and install updates |
58: | **Force update** | `devin update --force` | Re-install even if on latest version |
59: 
60: **Platform support:**
61: 
62: | Platform | Status |
63: |----------|--------|
64: | macOS | Full support (sandbox via Seatbelt, works out of the box) |
65: | Linux | Full support (sandbox requires `bwrap` + `socat`) |
66: | Windows (WSL) | Use WSL 2; native Windows cannot run the sandbox |
67: 
68: After installation, run `devin` for the interactive REPL or `devin -p -- "prompt"` for non-interactive use.
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ## 3. AUTHENTICATION
73: 
74: cli-devin authenticates through **Devin account OAuth only** — `devin auth login` (browser flow). It does not use an API key.
75: 
76: **OAuth login/logout:**
77: 
78: ```bash
79: # Authenticate via Devin account (opens browser)
80: devin auth login
81: 
82: # For SSH/remote sessions (skip browser, manually paste token)
83: devin auth login --force-manual-token-flow
84: 
85: # View authentication status
86: devin auth status
87: 
88: # Log out and clear stored credentials
89: devin auth logout
90: ```
91: 
92: **Auth status output:**
93: 
94: ```
95: Logged in (via Devin).
96: 
97: Credentials:
98:   File:              ~/.local/share/devin/credentials.toml
99:   API server:        https://server.codeium.com
100:   Devin webapp:      https://app.devin.ai
101:   Devin API:         https://api.devin.ai
102: ```
103: 
104: ---
105: 
106: ## 4. COMMAND-LINE FLAGS
107: 
108: ### Essential Flags
109: 
110: | Flag | Short | Values | Description |
111: |------|-------|--------|-------------|
112: | `--model` | | `<model-name>` | Model to use — `swe` (default alias → `swe-2`), plus the curated DeepSeek / GLM-5.2 / GPT-5.6 Luna Max / GPT-6 Luna Max / Grok (4.5 and 4.6) / SWE-2 families (see §5) |
113: | `--permission-mode` | | canonical: `normal`, `accept-edits`, `smart`, `dangerous`, `autonomous` — aliases: `auto`→`normal`, `yolo`/`bypass`→`dangerous` | Permission mode controlling tool auto-approval. **`devin --help` prints only 4 of these 8 accepted values** — it is not the authoritative enum. See the probe below. |
114: | `--print` | `-p` | `[<prompt>]` | Non-interactive mode: print response and exit |
115: | `--continue` | `-c` | (none) | Continue the most recent session in the current directory |
116: | `--resume` | `-r` | `[<session-id>]` | Resume a specific session by ID, or select interactively |
117: | `--sandbox` | | (none) | Enable OS-level process sandboxing (selects `autonomous` permission mode) |
118: | `--prompt-file` | | `<file>` | Load the initial prompt from a file |
119: | `--config` | | `<path>` | Configuration file path (override default `~/.config/devin/config.json`) |
120: | `--export` | | `[<path>]` | Export conversation to a file after each turn (ATIF format) |
121: | `--agent-config` | | `<file>` | Declarative agent configuration file (JSON or YAML) |
122: | `--respect-workspace-trust` | | `true`, `false` | Respect workspace trust settings |
123: 
124: > **Verifying a flag value without spending a session.** `--help` under-reports the
125: > `--permission-mode` enum, so never conclude a value is invalid because help omits it.
126: > Force parse-time validation instead: an invalid value fails at exit 2 before the file
127: > is read, a valid one reaches the file error at exit 1.
128: >
129: > ```bash
130: > devin --permission-mode <value> --prompt-file /nonexistent
131: > #   exit 2 + "invalid value ..."        -> rejected by the binary
132: > #   exit 1 + "Failed to read prompt file" -> accepted
133: > ```
134: >
135: > Verified against `devin 3000.6.7`: `auto`, `normal`, `accept-edits`, `smart`,
136: > `dangerous`, `yolo`, `bypass`, `autonomous` all accepted; `plan` and `manual`
137: > (Claude's modes, not Devin's) rejected. Re-run the probe after a CLI upgrade —
138: > `smart` was rejected at 3000.2.17 and is accepted at 3000.6.7.
139:

141: 
142: ```bash
143: # Interactive REPL (no prompt)
144: devin
145: 
146: # Start REPL with initial prompt (use -- before the prompt)
147: devin -- your prompt here
148: 
149: # Non-interactive: print mode
150: devin -p -- "prompt"

73:

81:

87:

90: ```

97: 
98: Dispatch this mode's default without opening any other file:
99:

102: | Default model | `swe` (alias → `swe-2`) |
103: | Default permission mode | `--permission-mode accept-edits` |
104: | Prompt separator | `--` before the print-mode prompt (required) |
105: 
106: If Devin is not authenticated (`devin auth status` not "logged in"), the mode ASKS the operator to run `devin auth login`. It never substitutes a different auth method or a model the user did not approve. See the auth pre-flight decision tree in [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md) §3.
107: 
108: ```bash
109: devin -p \
110:   --model swe \
111:   --permission-mode accept-edits \
112:   -- \
113:   "<prompt>"
114: ```
115: 
116: ---
117: 
118: ## 4. REASONING-EFFORT / THINKING LEVER
119: 
120: cli-devin has **no headless reasoning-effort flag**. There is no `--variant` (OpenCode 1 only) or `--effort` equivalent for non-interactive `devin -p` dispatch, and OpenCode 2 carries the level on the model id instead (`-m provider/model#<level>`). Two distinct levers stand in its place:
121: 
122: **1. Permission mode (`--permission-mode`), the autonomy lever.** This is what a dispatch actually controls: how much the agent may do without asking, not how hard it "thinks." Choose the least-permissive mode that lets the task complete.
123: 
124: | Mode | Flag | Behavior | Best for |
125: |------|------|----------|----------|
126: | Auto | `--permission-mode auto` | Auto-approves read-only tools and prompts for writes AND shell | Reading and summarising only (`devin -p` default). NOT a research crawl: see the warning below |
127: | Accept Edits | `--permission-mode accept-edits` | Auto-approves workspace edits + read-only, and prompts for shell | Code generation, refactoring (**skill default**) |
128: | Smart | `--permission-mode smart` | Auto-runs actions a fast model judges safe | Trusted workflows with judgment calls |
129: | Dangerous | `--permission-mode dangerous` | Auto-approves all tools without prompting | Full trust. **Requires explicit user approval** |
130: 
131: > **Headless, a prompt is a refusal.** `devin -p` defaults to `auto`, and in print mode there is
132: > nobody to answer a prompt, so the tool call is rejected and the run exits 0 having done nothing.
133: > That makes `auto` wrong for any task that must run a command, a research crawl included: observed
134: > 2026-09-15, a crawl dispatched on `auto` returned success with no findings. Use `auto` only when
135: > reading and summarising is genuinely the whole task. File modification needs `accept-edits` or
136: > higher for the same reason.
137: 
138: `--sandbox` is orthogonal containment, not a fifth permission mode. It enables Devin's OS sandboxing and does not select an additional `--permission-mode` value. Combine it with one of the four modes above when containment is required. This separation matches the live `devin --help` surface.
139: 
140: **2. Model thinking level, interactive only.** Some models support configurable reasoning depth, but it is **not exposed as a headless flag**. In an interactive REPL session, cycle the thinking level with `Alt+T` (macOS: `Opt+T`), or switch the interactive model with `/model <name>` / `Alt+T`. For non-interactive `-p` dispatch, choose the depth by picking the model instead: `deepseek-v4-flash-max` or `gpt-5-6-luna-max` for deep/max reasoning, `glm-5-2-max` for strong generation, and `swe-1-7-lightning` for minimal. The Max thinking tier is baked into the uid (`…-max`). The Fast speed tier is the `-priority` suffix (e.g. `gpt-5-6-luna-max-priority`), not a separate flag.
141: 
142: ---
143: 
144: ## 5. HOW TO INVOKE
145: 
146: ### Dispatch envelope (child / detached sessions)
147: When dispatching as a non-interactive child (spec-gate-neutralized worker), prefix the shared env, keep the `--` separator, and terminate stdin:
148: 
149: ```bash
150: SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1 devin -p \
151:   --model swe --permission-mode accept-edits \
152:   -- "<prompt>" </dev/null > stdout.log 2> stderr.log
153: ```
154: 
155: - `SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1`: neutralizes the spec-gate for a bound child worker so it does not stall waiting on an interactive Gate-3 answer, and marks the dispatch as an orchestrated sub-session so the worktree wrapper shares the parent worktree (SKILL.md §4 rules 15–16).
156: - `--` before the prompt is REQUIRED. Without it the prompt can be parsed as CLI flags.
157: - `</dev/null` is REQUIRED before stdout/stderr redirects (and inside any `while read` loop). `devin -p` inherits the caller's stdin and silently drains it, dropping later dispatches. See [integration-patterns.md](./integration-patterns.md) §4.
158: 
159: ### Self-invocation guard
160: A devin dispatch must not recursively re-enter a session already running inside Devin. The guard is packet-local and inline. See [../ROUTER.md](../ROUTER.md) §3 "Self-Invocation Guard" (detects `$DEVIN_PROJECT_DIR`, `devin` process ancestry, and active-session credentials).
161: 
162: ### Cloud handoff
163: Devin's unique `/handoff` transfers the current session to a cloud VM (own shell, browser, full repo access) for long-running, browser-dependent, or CI-like work. See [cloud-handoff.md](./cloud-handoff.md).
164: 
165: ### Parallel / fan-out
166: Multi-lineage parallel dispatch is driven by `fanout-run.cjs` (executor kind `cli-devin`), which lives outside this hub. See §6.
167: 
168: ---
169: 
170: ## 6. ENFORCEMENT & PROFILES (authoritative elsewhere, do not duplicate here)
171: 
172: - **Fan-out dispatcher + model enforcement** → `.skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/scripts/fanout-run.cjs` (executor kind `cli-devin`)
173: - **Live model ids** → `devin models` on the target install

81: - **DeepSeek Max tiers + GPT-5.6 Luna Max join (2026-08-14).** `deepseek-v4-flash-max` (the Max thinking tier of the DeepSeek V4 Flash family) and `gpt-5-6-luna-max` + `gpt-5-6-luna-max-priority` (the first GPT-5.6 persona in this catalog) were confirmed present verbatim in the live `devin models list` output on 2026-08-14. Devin encodes the "Fast" speed tier as the `-priority` suffix, not `-fast`, so `gpt-5-6-luna-max-priority` is the Fast variant of Luna Max. These four were **list-verified only, not dispatch-tested** (operator decision).
82: - **GPT-6 Luna Max joins (2026-09-24).** `gpt-6-luna-max` and `gpt-6-luna-max-priority` were confirmed verbatim in the live `devin models list` on devin 3000.11.1, which lists GPT-6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Luna as separate families, so the GPT-5.6 pair stays. `gpt-6-luna-max-priority` is dispatch-tested: a direct `devin -p` call returned a live reply at exit 0. `gpt-6-luna-max` is list-verified only.
83: - **DeepSeek Flash is Max-thinking-only (policy).** Dispatch DeepSeek V4 Flash only via `deepseek-v4-flash-max`. On devin the max thinking tier is baked into the uid, and this roster carries no bare `deepseek-v4-flash`. The sibling cli-pi and cli-opencode surfaces reach the same tier through a flag; their fan-out builders pin `deepseek-v4-flash` to max thinking:
84:   - cli-pi passes `--thinking max`.
85:   - On OpenCode 1 the same pin is `--variant max`.
86:   - On OpenCode 2 it rides on the model id instead (`-m provider/model#max`), so a v2 reader confirms that `opencode models --standalone` lists the `<provider>/` prefix of the model you pass to `-m` first.
87: 
88: **Gemini 3.8 Flash High retired from cli-devin (2026-09-06).** The uid `gemini-3-8-flash-high` was in scope from 2026-08-15 and is now rejected by the fan-out allowlist: Devin bills it at twice the 3.7 rate and a single two-iteration research pass exhausted the daily quota. Gemini 3.8 Flash High stays reachable through the cursor route. Do not dispatch it through Devin.
89: 
90: - GLM tier suffixes stack: `-max` = Max reasoning, `-1m` = 1M context, `-none` = reasoning disabled. `glm-5-2` (no suffix) is GLM-5.2 High (free tier).
91: - This is a curated subset. Devin's full 48-family roster (Claude, GPT, other Gemini, Kimi, older SWE, Fusion pairings, and the `adaptive` router) is available via `devin models list` but is out of this catalog's scope.

93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 3. DEFAULTS & QUICK INVOCATION
97: 
98: Dispatch this mode's default without opening any other file:
99: 
100: | Field | Value |
101: |-------|-------|
102: | Default model | `swe` (alias → `swe-2`) |
103: | Default permission mode | `--permission-mode accept-edits` |
104: | Prompt separator | `--` before the print-mode prompt (required) |
105: 
106: If Devin is not authenticated (`devin auth status` not "logged in"), the mode ASKS the operator to run `devin auth login`. It never substitutes a different auth method or a model the user did not approve. See the auth pre-flight decision tree in [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md) §3.
107: 
108: ```bash
109: devin -p \
110:   --model swe \
111:   --permission-mode accept-edits \
112:   -- \
113:   "<prompt>"
114: ```
115: 
116: ---
117: 
118: ## 4. REASONING-EFFORT / THINKING LEVER
119: 
120: cli-devin has **no headless reasoning-effort flag**. There is no `--variant` (OpenCode 1 only) or `--effort` equivalent for non-interactive `devin -p` dispatch, and OpenCode 2 carries the level on the model id instead (`-m provider/model#<level>`). Two distinct levers stand in its place:
121: 
122: **1. Permission mode (`--permission-mode`), the autonomy lever.** This is what a dispatch actually controls: how much the agent may do without asking, not how hard it "thinks." Choose the least-permissive mode that lets the task complete.
123: 
124: | Mode | Flag | Behavior | Best for |
125: |------|------|----------|----------|
126: | Auto | `--permission-mode auto` | Auto-approves read-only tools and prompts for writes AND shell | Reading and summarising only (`devin -p` default). NOT a research crawl: see the warning below |
127: | Accept Edits | `--permission-mode accept-edits` | Auto-approves workspace edits + read-only, and prompts for shell | Code generation, refactoring (**skill default**) |
128: | Smart | `--permission-mode smart` | Auto-runs actions a fast model judges safe | Trusted workflows with judgment calls |
129: | Dangerous | `--permission-mode dangerous` | Auto-approves all tools without prompting | Full trust. **Requires explicit user approval** |
130: 
131: > **Headless, a prompt is a refusal.** `devin -p` defaults to `auto`, and in print mode there is
132: > nobody to answer a prompt, so the tool call is rejected and the run exits 0 having done nothing.
133: > That makes `auto` wrong for any task that must run a command, a research crawl included: observed
134: > 2026-09-15, a crawl dispatched on `auto` returned success with no findings. Use `auto` only when
135: > reading and summarising is genuinely the whole task. File modification needs `accept-edits` or
136: > higher for the same reason.
137: 
138: `--sandbox` is orthogonal containment, not a fifth permission mode. It enables Devin's OS sandboxing and does not select an additional `--permission-mode` value. Combine it with one of the four modes above when containment is required. This separation matches the live `devin --help` surface.
139: 
140: **2. Model thinking level, interactive only.** Some models support configurable reasoning depth, but it is **not exposed as a headless flag**. In an interactive REPL session, cycle the thinking level with `Alt+T` (macOS: `Opt+T`), or switch the interactive model with `/model <name>` / `Alt+T`. For non-interactive `-p` dispatch, choose the depth by picking the model instead: `deepseek-v4-flash-max` or `gpt-5-6-luna-max` for deep/max reasoning, `glm-5-2-max` for strong generation, and `swe-1-7-lightning` for minimal. The Max thinking tier is baked into the uid (`…-max`). The Fast speed tier is the `-priority` suffix (e.g. `gpt-5-6-luna-max-priority`), not a separate flag.
141: 
142: ---
143: 
144: ## 5. HOW TO INVOKE
145: 
146: ### Dispatch envelope (child / detached sessions)
147: When dispatching as a non-interactive child (spec-gate-neutralized worker), prefix the shared env, keep the `--` separator, and terminate stdin:
148: 
149: ```bash
150: SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1 devin -p \
151:   --model swe --permission-mode accept-edits \
152:   -- "<prompt>" </dev/null > stdout.log 2> stderr.log
153: ```
154: 
155: - `SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1`: neutralizes the spec-gate for a bound child worker so it does not stall waiting on an interactive Gate-3 answer, and marks the dispatch as an orchestrated sub-session so the worktree wrapper shares the parent worktree (SKILL.md §4 rules 15–16).
156: - `--` before the prompt is REQUIRED. Without it the prompt can be parsed as CLI flags.
157: - `</dev/null` is REQUIRED before stdout/stderr redirects (and inside any `while read` loop). `devin -p` inherits the caller's stdin and silently drains it, dropping later dispatches. See [integration-patterns.md](./integration-patterns.md) §4.
158: 
159: ### Self-invocation guard
160: A devin dispatch must not recursively re-enter a session already running inside Devin. The guard is packet-local and inline. See [../ROUTER.md](../ROUTER.md) §3 "Self-Invocation Guard" (detects `$DEVIN_PROJECT_DIR`, `devin` process ancestry, and active-session credentials).
161: 
162: ### Cloud handoff
163: Devin's unique `/handoff` transfers the current session to a cloud VM (own shell, browser, full repo access) for long-running, browser-dependent, or CI-like work. See [cloud-handoff.md](./cloud-handoff.md).
164: 
165: ### Parallel / fan-out
166: Multi-lineage parallel dispatch is driven by `fanout-run.cjs` (executor kind `cli-devin`), which lives outside this hub. See §6.

147: ### OS-Level Sandbox (--sandbox)
148: 
149: **Process sandboxing for autonomous execution.** The `--sandbox` flag enables OS-level sandboxing (macOS Seatbelt / Linux bwrap+seccomp) that enforces filesystem and network boundaries.
150: 
151: **Capabilities:**
152: - Shell commands and fetches auto-approve because the sandbox enforces what they can touch
153: - Direct file edits via `edit`/`write` tools still prompt (they run inside the CLI process, not the sandbox)
154: - Scopes granted mid-session dynamically expand the sandbox
155: - Domain allow/deny lists filter network access
156: - Only available with `autonomous` permission mode
157: 
158: **Platform requirements:**
159: - macOS: works out of the box via Seatbelt
160: - Linux: requires `bwrap` and `socat` (run `devin sandbox setup` for prerequisites)
161: - Windows: use WSL 2 (native Windows cannot run the sandbox)
162: 
163: **Usage:**
164: 
165: ```bash
166: # Autonomous mode with OS-enforced sandbox

194: ### Silent Stdin Consumption When Dispatching in a `while read` Loop
195: 
196: When a dispatcher script iterates over lines of input with `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < input.jsonl` and launches `devin -p ... &` inside the loop body, **devin silently consumes the loop's stdin**. The loop exits after the first 3-6 iterations with no error, dropping most dispatches.
197: 
198: **Symptom:** You dispatch a 27-finding batch; only 3-6 devin processes actually launch. No error, no warning.
199: 
200: **Root cause:** `devin -p` inherits the script's stdin by default. Each backgrounded devin process reads from the same file descriptor and races with the `read` command for lines.
201: 
202: **Always pair `devin -p ... &` inside a read-loop with `</dev/null` on the redirection.**
203: 
204: ```bash
205: # BAD: devin inherits the loop's stdin, drains input.jsonl after iteration ~3
206: while IFS= read -r line; do
207:   devin -p "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 &
208:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
209: done < input.jsonl
210: 
211: # GOOD: redirect devin stdin from /dev/null so the loop keeps its own
212: while IFS= read -r line; do
213:   devin -p "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &
214:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
215: done < input.jsonl
216: ```
